newsitem.title: FRANCE: French give left strong lead in warning to Chirac.
newsitem.headline: French give left strong lead in warning to Chirac.

text.p: French voters sent a severe warning to President Jacques Chirac on Sunday, giving a jubilant left a substantial lead over the ruling centre-right coalition in the first round of a parliamentary election.

The massive protest vote after two years of austerity and record unemployment under Prime Minister Alain Juppe threw next Sunday's decisive second-round runoff wide open and put the left within reach of a stunning upset, polling institutes said.

Projections by the three major polling firms suggested France could be heading for a period of difficult "cohabitation" between a left-wing government dependent on Communist votes and the conservative Chirac, who called the snap election in hopes of ensuring himself a majority for his remaining five years in office.

The opposition Socialists, Communists, extreme-left and other-left candidates were set to capture about 41 percent of the first-round vote, with the ruling RPR-UDF coalition and other moderate-right candidates scoring around 36.5 percent.
The extreme-right, anti-immigration National Front was on course for its best parliamentary score with about 15 percent. Its leader, Jean-Marie Le Pen, called on Chirac to resign.
A record number of votes were cast for fringe, ecologist or extremist parties. Turnout was about 68 percent, barely less than in 1993 despite voter disenchantment.

The risk of a left-wing victory sent the deutschemark higher against several European currencies in rare Sunday night trading. Economists forecast a nervous reaction to the left's strong showing when French financial markets open on Monday.
Juppe, whose deep unpopularity was a key factor, sought to put a brave face on his side's mediocre result in a brief statement at coalition headquarters.

"The French people meant above all to say that they want a real change. We must listen to this message." he said. Pledging a renewed drive to modernise France for the 21st century, he urged the right to mobilise all efforts to win the second round.
Juppe scored a poor 38.6 percent in his own constituency in Bordeaux and was forced into a runoff by a Socialist rival.

Several coalition leaders described the vote as a "warning" and said the right must heed the voters' message, but no one called openly for Chirac to dump Juppe and promise a different prime minister to secure a conservative victory.

Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin, sounding more cautious than his cheering supporters, said the vote showed a new, left-wing majority was possible and appealed to the left to unite for victory next Sunday.

"I call on all those who want a more balanced government and a new policy for France to unite on this second round. All those who aspire to change must unite because a change of majority is possible and desirable," he said in a statement in his constituency of Cintegabelle, near Toulouse.
Communist leader Robert Hue said Chirac had sought a vote of confidence and the French people had told him "No!". He promised the Communists would fight all-out for a left-wing victory.
Most of the 577 National Assembly seats were set to go to a runoff, where the behaviour of National Front supporters and of the roughly 32 percent of voters who abstained will be crucial.

The SOFRES polling firm forecast that the RPR-UDF coalition would win 255-287 seats next Sunday, short of the 289 required for a parliamentary majority. It projected the Socialists would win 250-270 seats, their Communist allies 21-30 seats and the National Front 0-3 seats.
The BVA institute put the RPR-UDF between 255 and 275, well short of a majority, with the Socialists taking 250 to 270, the Communists 15-20 and the National Front 0-2.
The projections could leave the Communists holding the balance of power or even give a tiny handful of extreme-right deputies a pivotal position.

"The arithmetic tonight is really favourable to the left yet it remains really open for next Sunday," veteran political analyst Alain Duhamel said, noting that the centre-right appeared to have larger reserves of voters to mobilise.
The vote was a severe blow to Chirac, who wagered the future of his presidency after two years in office on the snap poll, 10 months before his giant parliamentary majority needed to face voters.
Chirac said he took the decision because he needed a "new elan" to lead France into a single European currency, a policy rejected by both the Communists and the National Front.

The coalition promised market-oriented reforms to scale down state control, cut taxes and free up private enterprise. The left pledged vigorous state job creation and a shorter working week to attack record 12.8 percent joblessness.
A total 6,389 candidates, including a record 1,469 women, vied on Sunday for seats in the chamber.
